As of 315 AM EDT Friday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Record to near record warmth and breezy today with 
gusty showers (isolated thunderstorms) possible along a strong cold 
front tonight into Saturday morning. 

Early this morning, a shallow backdoor cold front that pushed south 
yesterday has stalled across the Carolinas and is beginning to lift 
back northward as a warm front. Satellite and surface observations 
show low stratus and patchy fog in the wake of the front due to a 
light onshore flow. In addition, light to moderate rain showers have 
developed across northern portions of the forecast area, with the 
highest coverage from the Northern Neck over to the MD Eastern 
Shore. Any low clouds and/or fog dissipates rather quickly later 
this morning as the front lifts north as a warm front and winds 
become southerly. 

An expansive deep upper trough digging across the Great Lakes into 
the Ohio Valley today will drive rapid, low-level warm air advection 
over the Mid Atlantic. Highs will soar into the mid to upper 80s 
this afternoon, with a few spots potentially approaching 90F (upper 
70s to lower 80s at the immediate Atlantic coast and across the 
Eastern Shore). These values are ~15 to 20 degrees above normal and 
will challenge record highs, see the climate section below for more 
details. 

Still expecting the daytime hours to remain dry area-wide. A strong 
cold front approaches from the NW this evening, and is forecast to 
cross the area late tonight into Saturday morning. CAMs still depict 
a thin, strongly forced line of showers and isolated storms late 
this evening into tonight. The overnight timing and limited 
instability (MLCAPE ~500 J/kg or less) should keep the overall 
severe threat low for a majority of the area. However, strong 
kinematics aloft will likely be able to mix down to the surface with 
wind gusts of 30 to 40+ mph possible as the front comes through. We 
will need to keep an eye on far northeastern portions of the area 
(MD Eastern Shore) where there may be slightly better instability 
and better kinematics. SPC has this area highlighted in a Slight 
Risk (level 2 out of 5) with a Marginal Risk (1 out of 5) for areas 
north of I-64 for the potential for strong to severe wind gusts. The 
best dynamics for severe storms will likely be north of the local 
area. 

For Saturday, the front crosses the area and moves off the coast by 
the morning, triggering a sharp surge of cold air advection. Daytime 
highs will be achieved during the early morning hours, with 
temperatures struggling to get out of the mid 50s by the afternoon 
hours. Deep mixing in the wake of the front will promote breezy NW 
winds, with gusts of 25 to 35+ mph inland and 40 to 45+ mph along 
the immediate coast. Rain chances hang on into the late 
morning/early afternoon hours (highest SE) as the upper shortwave 
does not cross the area until 18z or later. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Much cooler temperatures arrive this weekend, with 
frost possible Sunday morning, mainly in the Piedmont.

Strong NW flow aloft in the wake of the cold front will usher in the 
coolest airmass of the season Saturday night into Sunday.
Strong sfc high pressure builds east from the OH Valley, but there 
will likely be a decent pressure gradient locally, especially closer 
to the coast. With the surface high forecast to be 1035mb+, kept the 
theme from the previous forecast and undercut NBM lows by a few 
degrees in the northern Piedmont where decoupling is more probable 
closer to sunrise (lows into the mid 30s). Depending on dewpoints, 
at least patchy frost will be possible there. Closer to the coast, 
lows will range from the upper 40s to mid 50s. Mostly sunny Sunday 
(potentially more clouds in the SE) with highs about 10 degrees 
below normal, in the upper 50s to lower 60s. Additional frost 
potential is possible Sunday night into Monday morning across the 
northern Piedmont with temperatures again dropping back into the 
30s. 


KEY MESSAGE 3...There still remains a lot of uncertainty for next 
week with a potential strong coastal system lingering offshore or 
retrograding back towards the local area.

Considerable ensemble/deterministic model spread exists heading into 
early to mid next week. Strong high pressure wedges down from the 
north, while an upper cutoff low develops off the Southeast/Mid 
Atlantic coast. Guidance continues to struggle with how close this 
coastal system remains to the shoreline, with some solutions having 
this low retrograding back towards the local area by mid to late 
week. For now, have low end (slight chance) rain chances along the 
immediate coast through much of next week, but this will be refined 
as models get a better handle on this coastal system. Breezy N to NE 
winds will likely persist through much of next week, with the 
highest gusts along the immediate coast. Near to slightly below 
average temperatures are currently in the forecast for next week.
